title: Earth Is Changing: Follow the Arrows
body:
Your mission is to explain two different kinds of change: building or moving land, and changing how much land water covers. They can work over very long periods. One drawing cannot explain the whole history of every Philippine island.

A tectonic plate is a large, solid piece of Earth's outer layer. Plates move slowly compared with everyday journeys. They can move toward one another, apart, or past one another. Their interactions can shape mountains, trenches and volcanic regions.

Read the arrows in the three-panel model. They show kinds of movement, not actual Philippine plate boundaries. Rocks and measured movement help scientists investigate these processes. A classroom diagram shows an idea; it is not itself a measurement of an island's age.
clues: Toward each other
In panel A, the arrowheads point toward the meeting line. This represents plates moving together.
Away from each other
Panel B has arrows pointing away from the meeting line. It represents plates moving apart.
Along the meeting line
Panel C has opposite arrows along the meeting line. It represents plates sliding past one another.
task: Panel B has arrows pointing away from the meeting line. Which movement does it represent?
Plates moving apart
Plates moving together
Plates staying still
Ocean water falling
reason: The arrowheads in panel B point away from the meeting line. They represent plates moving apart, not a change in sea level.

title: Watch How: Volcanic Material Can Build Land
body:
Watch a worked explanation using three stages. Magma is molten rock below the surface. When it reaches the surface, it is called lava. Volcanic material can cool and become rock. Material can build up over repeated events.

Step 1. Find the material coming through an opening. Step 2. Compare the smaller pile with the larger pile. Step 3. Explain the change: repeated additions of material can build land.

The stages simplify a process. They do not say how long every volcano takes to grow, and an eruption can also damage or remove land. Volcanism is part of the Philippines' complex geological history; not every island is one volcano. This diagram is for learning, not a prediction about a real eruption.
clues: Below the surface
The first stage labels magma below an opening. Magma and a solid tectonic plate are not the same thing.
Material at the surface
The second stage labels lava at the surface. Cooling volcanic material can add rock.
Compare the stages
The larger pile in stage three represents accumulated material. It does not mean every eruption makes exactly the same amount.
task: A model shows repeated additions of cooled volcanic material. What process does this demonstrate?
Volcanic material accumulating to build land
Sea level falling without new rock
All land forming in a single event
A plate changing into ocean water
reason: The model adds material at the surface over repeated stages. This illustrates one land-building process, not the origin of every island.

title: Try Together: Shallow Shelf or Deep Channel?
body:
Now compare water coverage rather than adding rock. A continental shelf is a shallow, submerged edge of a continent. When sea level is lower, some shallow areas can be exposed. A coastline is where land meets the sea; that meeting place can move when water level changes.

Worked example: look at the shallow ledge in both panels. The model keeps the land shape unchanged. Only the water level falls. Some of the ledge becomes exposed, so more land is visible without new rock being made.

Next check the deep channel. It still contains water in the lower-water panel. Lower seas did not make every Philippine island one continuous bridge. This is a made-up cross-section, not a map of a particular ancient connection. A claim about a real route needs site-specific evidence.
clues: What stayed the same?
The brown land outline matches in both panels. This model is not showing new volcanic material.
What became exposed?
The lower blue water line leaves part of the shallow ledge above water. The shoreline changes position.
What remains underwater?
The deep channel remains below even the lower water line. Less water does not necessarily remove every gap.
task: In the lower-water panel, the shallow ledge is exposed but the deep channel remains flooded. Which conclusion fits?
More land is exposed, but a water gap remains
Every island must now join into one landmass
New lava has made the shallow ledge
The land outline has to disappear
reason: Lowering water can expose shallow land while deeper channels remain underwater. This model does not prove a bridge connecting all Philippine islands.

title: Your Turn: Choose the Evidence
body:
A scientific explanation connects observations with an explanation that can be checked. A theory in science is not simply a random guess. Scientists compare evidence, test ideas and revise explanations when needed.

Try this made-up research problem. A team proposes that a shallow coastal area was once exposed. The team needs evidence about past water levels, rock layers and land shape at that place. A drawing alone cannot prove the proposal.

An observation describes what was recorded. An interpretation explains what it may mean. A model simplifies an idea. These help one another but are not interchangeable. If a model conflicts with good evidence, investigate and improve it rather than hide the disagreement.
clues: Observation card
A research notebook records the location and type of a rock sample. This is an observation, not a complete explanation of all islands.
Interpretation card
The team suggests that a layer formed under different water conditions. That explanation must be checked against the sample and other observations.
Model card
The two-panel illustration leaves many details out. Its job is to show how changing water coverage could work.
task: A new measurement does not fit the team's model. What should the team do?
Check the measurement and revise the model if the evidence supports it
Keep the model because the picture is attractive
Replace the measurement with a made-up one
Call the model a direct photograph of the past
reason: Models explain selected ideas. Scientists check measurements and improve an explanation when reliable evidence calls for a change.

title: Compare Sources Respectfully
body:
People ask different questions about origins. Geological investigations ask how physical processes shape land. Traditional origin stories can express meaning, values and identity within a community. Learning their different purposes helps us discuss both respectfully.

Our source cards are classroom descriptions, not an authentic traditional story. Card A describes measurements of rock and land. Card B describes a community story being shared with its meaning and permission explained.

For a question about how rock formed, examine physical evidence and scientific methods. For a question about what a story means to its community, listen to an appropriately attributed account. Respect does not mean treating every source as a geological measurement, and scientific study does not require mocking a tradition.
clues: Question about a process
Card A suits a question about changes to rock and land because it describes physical observations.
Question about meaning
Card B suits a question about the values expressed in a story. Its community, source and sharing context matter.
Keep the label honest
An invented classroom description must not be labelled as an actual ancient community story. These cards do not reproduce one.
task: A class asks what values a traditional origin story expresses. Which source is most suitable?
An attributed community account explaining the story's meaning
Only a measurement of the coastline
An invented story labelled as authentic
Only the colour used in a volcano diagram
reason: The question concerns a story's meaning, so an appropriately attributed community account is relevant. Rock measurements answer a different kind of question.

title: Field Journal: Explain Two Kinds of Change
body:
Return to the mission problem. Building or moving land is different from changing how much existing land is covered by water. Your explanation should say which process the evidence supports.

Connect three ideas. Plates are moving parts of Earth's solid outer layer. Volcanic material can accumulate and build rock. A change in sea level can expose or cover existing shallow land without adding that rock. Several processes matter across the Philippines' long geological history.

Before the quiz, practise this sentence: I think this model shows ___ because I notice ___. Then add one limit, such as: this model is not a map of every island. Revisit the relevant diagram if the processes are confusing. Authored help remains available without AI.
clues: Look for new material
A growing pile of cooled volcanic material supports an explanation about adding rock.
Look for changed coverage
An unchanged land shape and a lower water line support an explanation about water coverage.
State a limit
Neither classroom model shows the full geological history of all Philippine islands or predicts a real eruption.
task: Two drawings keep the land shape identical but lower the water line. Which explanation fits?
Existing land becomes exposed as sea level falls
New volcanic rock must have been added
The drawing proves every island was joined
Plate movement has stopped everywhere
reason: The unchanged land and different water line show exposure of existing land, not new rock. The simplified model cannot establish every ancient island connection.
